title: Fascia iliaca / femoral nerve block
stem: Cubicle 21. Mrs Ma, 84 (50 kg), has a fractured neck of femur. She is in severe pain despite paracetamol. Perform an ultrasound-guided fascia iliaca block on the model.

review.text: Local anaesthetic dose. Your notes give 20–30 mL of 0.5% ropivacaine or 0.25–0.5% bupivacaine. Check the total against weight: 30 mL of 0.5% is 150 mg, over 2 mg/kg in a 50 kg woman. Use a larger volume of a more dilute solution within the maximum dose, and label the patient with the drug and time.

notes:
Checked against NICE CG124 (Hip fracture, updated 2023), the Association of Anaesthetists / RCEM safety guideline for fascia iliaca blocks in the ED (2021), and the AAGBI guideline for local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST, 2010).

NICE recommends nerve blocks (fascia iliaca or femoral) for hip fracture pain in the ED, alongside paracetamol and cautious opioids. The ultrasound-guided fascia iliaca compartment block deposits a large volume of dilute local anaesthetic under the fascia iliaca, lateral to the femoral nerve, spreading to the femoral and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves (and sometimes obturator). Safety: consent, check allergies and anticoagulation, weight-based dose (e.g. levobupivacaine 0.25% up to 2 mg/kg, or 30–40 mL of a dilute solution staying within the maximum dose), monitoring, IV access, aspirate before injecting in 5 mL increments, lipid emulsion available, document, and a sign on the patient (time and drug) to avoid repeat dosing.

Your notes describe a femoral nerve block with 20–30 mL ropivacaine 0.5% or bupivacaine 0.25–0.5%; check the total dose against weight (0.5% × 30 mL = 150 mg — over 2 mg/kg in a 50 kg woman). The rest (NAVEL, in-plane, hydrodissection, aspiration, LAST readiness) matches.

steps.label: Safety checks
steps.hint: Consent, allergy, anticoagulants, weight and maximum dose, monitoring, IV, lipid emulsion.

opts.t: Consent; allergy to local anaesthetic; anticoagulants
Weigh her: 50 kg; maximum levobupivacaine 2 mg/kg = 100 mg
Monitoring and IV access; 20% lipid emulsion on the trolley
opts.mark: Monitoring, IV access and lipid emulsion available

opts.t: Check she hasn't had a block from the ambulance crew

steps.label: Ultrasound-guided block
steps.hint: Probe below the inguinal ligament, identify artery, nerve, fascia iliaca, iliopsoas; in-plane lateral to medial; aspirate; inject in increments.

opts.t: Clean the groin; sterile probe cover
Linear probe transverse below the inguinal ligament: femoral artery, nerve lateral to it, fascia iliaca over iliopsoas
Needle in-plane from lateral to medial, tip under the fascia iliaca lateral to the nerve
opts.mark: In-plane approach with the tip under the fascia

opts.t: Aspirate; inject 2 mL and watch the fascia lift (hydrodissection)
Inject 40 mL of 0.25% levobupivacaine (100 mg) in 5 mL aliquots, aspirating between
opts.mark: Incremental injection within the maximum dose

opts.t: Document; label the time and drug on her wrist; observe for LAST
Inject quickly without seeing the needle tip
opts.r: Risk of intravascular or intraneural injection. Always see the tip.

qs.a: Perioral tingling, tinnitus, agitation, then seizures
wrong: Isolated bradycardia with a normal ECG

qs.a: Stop, airway, treat seizures, 20% lipid 1.5 mL/kg
wrong: Adrenaline 1 mg IV at once, whatever the rhythm, then lipid

qs.q: Order of structures lateral to medial in the groin?
Nerves covered by a fascia iliaca block?
wrong: Sciatic, tibial and common peroneal nerves

qs.q: Why a sign on the patient's wrist after the block?
qs.a: To prevent a repeat dose over the maximum
wrong: It is required for billing the procedure
So the family know which leg was blocked and when
It is not needed; the notes are enough

badge.name: Iliac Relief
badge.flavor: Dose by weight, see the tip, aspirate, increments, lipid nearby.

cards.q: Hip fracture analgesia recommended by NICE in the ED?
options: No analgesia until theatre, to aid assessment

cards.q: The femoral nerve lies relative to the femoral artery…
Complication of femoral block to warn about?
options: Bradycardia from blockade of the vagus nerve
